newsitem.title: USA: Heinz expected to announce job cuts, charges.
newsitem.headline: Heinz expected to announce job cuts, charges.

text.p: H.J. Heinz Co., which for months has said it plans to restructure, is expected to cut its workforce by 6 percent and take a pretax charge of $500 million in its fiscal fourth quarter ended April 30, the Wall Street Journal reported on Monday.

The food giant is also expected to announce plans to sell ancillary businesses in the coming year, including poultry and ice cream units in New Zealand, and close manufacturing facilities in North America and Europe to cut costs, according to a report in Monday's Wall Street Journal.
A Heinz spokeswoman declined to confirm any details.

"We're not confirming anything at this point...we'll have more to say on Friday" when the company is scheduled to reveal the details of its restructuring plan before analysts in San Francisco. The company also is scheduled to release fiscal third quarter earnings that day.
Heinz officials have said for months the company will restructure to focus on its six core businesses and achieve double-digit growth, but have not disclosed details.
The six core segments are ketchup and condiments, tuna, weight control, pet food, infant food and food service.

Analysts said they are sceptical whether Heinz can achieve double-digit growth over a sustained period because the food industry has been growing at just 1 percent annually and producers have been unable to effectively raise prices.
But analysts said the press report was not surprising because Heinz officials have indicated those businesses could be sold.

William Johnson, Heinz's president, told Reuters in January the company was looking at selling ancillary units, including poultry and ice cream. Analysts also said Heinz's restructuring was in line with moves by its competitors, who also are selling businesses and cutting costs to stay competitive in a stagnating industry.

Steven Galbraith at Sanford C. Bernstein said Heinz can probably achieve double-digit growth for the next two fiscal years. "After that I think (the businesses) can grow by 8 to 10 percent," he said. "I think 10 to 12 percent is a stretch.
"They've done a decent job with what they have... I don't think any of the businesses will see dramatic growth."

"I don't think it's a big surprise. They're looking at businesses that account for 5 percent of sales. If you look at the food industry, they all want to grow 10 to 12 percent a year," said William Leach at Donaldson Lufkin & Jenrette.
"But the industry is growing at 1 percent a year... I think Heinz can achieve double-digit growth in the short term but not in the longer term," Leach said.
Heinz stock closed up 12.5 cents at $43.875 on the New York Stock Exchange.
